subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 15-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature, a webbed neck, and primary amenorrhea. Physical examination shows a shield chest with widely spaced nipples, and karyotyping reveals 45,X.
question: Which of the following is most likely when her buccal mucosal cells are examined for Barr bodies?

options.text: Two Barr bodies in each nucleus
One Barr body in each nucleus
No Barr bodies, because she has only one X chromosome
One Barr body in half of the cells and none in the other half
Barr bodies located within the mitochondria

explanation_correct: A Barr body is an inactive, condensed X chromosome, a form of methylated heterochromatin that is visible at the periphery of the nucleus. In XX cells one X is randomly inactivated, leaving one Barr body; a 45,X individual has only one X, so no X is inactivated and no Barr body is present.

explanation_incorrect.A: Two Barr bodies would require at least three X chromosomes, as in 47,XXX.
explanation_incorrect.B: One Barr body is the normal finding in 46,XX cells, but this patient has only a single X.
explanation_incorrect.D: Random inactivation still produces one Barr body per XX cell; it does not create a 50% mixture of cells with and without a Barr body.
explanation_incorrect.E: Barr bodies are nuclear, not mitochondrial; mitochondria have their own circular DNA that does not bind histones.

educationalObjective: The Barr body is the methylated, inactivated X chromosome; normal XX cells have one, whereas 45,X cells have none.
